newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Punjab polls marked by strange bedfellows.
newsitem.headline: India's Punjab polls marked by strange bedfellows.

text.p: Politics is making for strange bedfellows in India's Punjab state as the rich farming region, recovering from years of separatist strife, prepares to elect a new government, analysts said on Tuesday.

They noted that this Friday's assembly polls involving 117 seats were the first elections in nearly two decades not overshadowed by Sikh separatists fighting for a separate homeland called Khalistan, or Land of the Pure.
Politicians polled by Reuters said the elections will also be a test for India's experiment with coalition rule.

The rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), a strong critic of separatism, is fighting the elections in alliance with a faction of the Sikh Akali Dal party considered sympathetic to the separatists.
"You go to polls alone where you are strong on your own," BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj told Reuters. "In Punjab today nobody can claim to win an election on their own -- not the Akalis, not us."
"The polls reveal the difference between opportunism and principled politics," Swaraj said.
Congress officials were quick to accuse the BJP of hypocricy.

"The BJP has joined hands with the Akali Dal which has not given up its demand for a separate state," said Congress spokesman Ved Prakash. "With what face can the BJP claim to be a nationalist party?"

To add to the confusion, Punjab's ruling Congress party, which suffered its worst-ever defeat in national polls last year, has linked up with an unlikely partner in the Communist Party of India (CPI).
The two parties stay at a guarded distance in New Delhi.

Congress, which took power in 1992 in no small measure due to a boycott of the state elections by the Akali Dal, has been deserted in this week's polls by an important ally, a grouping of low caste Hindus and Sikhs led by the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP).

Congress and the BSP were partners in elections in India's most populous state of Uttar Pradesh last September which produced a hung assembly. The key northern state has been ruled directly by the federal government as a result of the impasse.

Swaraj said the Punjab elections would affect national politics, where the BJP was seeking to bring down Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's eight-month-old centre-left minority alliance in this month's budget session of parliament.
Analysts said the Akali Dal-BJP alliance was likely to wrest power from the Congress, unpopular among many Sikhs who blame former Congress prime minister Indira Gandhi for targeting their community.

Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards in October 1984, four months after she ordered troops into the Golden Temple at Amritsar, Sikhdom's holiest shrine, to flush out armed Sikh militants holed up there.
The assault on the Punjab shrine is regarded as the trigger for the bloody Sikh uprising against Indian rule in which more than 20,000 people died over the following decade.
Human rights groups have accused Indian troops in Punjab of large-scale rights abuses, including torture and murder. The government denies the allegations.

Indian officials say the insurgency has been largely quelled, but analysts say the assassination in August 1995 of Punjab's then Congress chief minister Beant Singh by a suspected suicide bomber indicates militancy still lurks in the wings.
